newsitem.title: BRAZIL: INTERVIEW-Brazil eyes role as LatAm stocks hub.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Brazil eyes role as LatAm stocks hub.

text.p: Local securities regulators hope the newly created Brazilian Depositary Receipts (BDRs) will turn Brazil into a financial hub for Latin America -- a mini-New York, so to speak.

"It offers an alternative for Latin American companies too small to trade in New York," said Elizabeth Garbayo, superintendent for market development for Brazil's Securities and Exchange Commission (CVM).
She said U.S.-based multinationals also have expressed interest in launching BDRs, but the market is more apt to draw from Argentina, Chile, Mexico and Peru.
"We foresee participation by companies in Mercosur as well as other parts of Latin America," Garbayo said.
She declined to name prospective BDR issuers, but said Brazilian market regulators have been contacted by investment banks and brokerages representing firms in Argentina, Mexico and Peru.
The CVM also was contacted directly about the program by companies in the United States, she said.

The government's main goal in creating BDRs, which were approved late Wednesday by the National Monetary Council, was to increase liquidity and revenues and boost often-sluggish trade in local stock markets.

Garbayo said BDRs will give Brazilians a chance to buy and sell foreign companies' stock and permit foreign firms with local subsidiaries, or those which do business in Brazil, to list on local bolsas.
But New York, London and other world financial meccas need not worry about losing business just yet.

Brazil's largest stock market, the Sao Paulo Stock Exchange, trades only an average $380 million on a cash basis daily, while second-largest Rio de Janeiro bolsa's daily volume is less than half that.
Both sums are small compared with major world markets.
No start-up date for trading of BDRs has been set yet.
Legislation governing the instrument is modeled on American Depositary Receipts (ADRs), which allow foreign firms to trade on United States markets.
Like their U.S. counterparts, BDRs would be available on three levels and carry virtually identical requirements, Garbayo said.
Many Latin American firms now trade in the U.S. and other global markets under ADR and GDR programs, including banks, power utilities and beer, food, mining, oil and telecommunications firms.
